result.summary: Jupiter sends Mercury to rouse Mars, and the Argive army, tricked by Panic, marches on Thebes while Jupiter calms Bacchus's plea for his city. Antigone and old Phorbas survey the Theban host from a tower, Jocasta fails to broker peace, a Fury drives Bacchus's tigers into the fight, and in battle Amphiaraus is swallowed alive by the earth.

scenes.title: Mercury Rouses Mars
scenes.summary: Jupiter sends Mercury to the iron house of Mars in Thrace to order him to start the war. Mars obeys and drives out.
scenes.stakes: Mercury risks Mars's wrath; Jupiter threatens to strip Mars of his power if he delays.

scenes.title: Vow and Panic at Nemea
scenes.summary: Adrastus vows to Archemorus, then Mars sends Panic to stir the Argives, who rush to arms.
scenes.stakes: The Argives risk the war's outcome through delay and then through blind panic.

scenes.title: Bacchus Pleads for Thebes
scenes.summary: Bacchus begs Jupiter to spare Thebes; Jupiter answers that fate demands the war but that Thebes will not fall now.
scenes.stakes: Bacchus fears the ruin of his native Thebes and its people.

scenes.title: Antigone and Phorbas on the Tower
scenes.summary: Eteocles gathers allies, and Phorbas names the Theban leaders to Antigone, telling tales of Alatreus, Hypseus and others.
scenes.stakes: Thebes faces invasion; old Phorbas grieves over Laius's death.

scenes.title: Eteocles Speaks; Argives Cross Asopus
scenes.summary: Eteocles orders his troops while the Argives march past dire omens, cross the swollen Asopus and camp.
scenes.stakes: Argives risk drowning and ignore divine warnings of doom.

scenes.title: Jocasta's Plea
scenes.summary: Jocasta goes to the Argive camp and begs Polynices to make peace; Tydeus talks the troops out of it, and the Fury stirs strife.
scenes.stakes: Jocasta risks losing both sons; Polynices risks betrayal if he enters Thebes.

scenes.title: Bacchus's Tigers and First Battle
scenes.summary: The Fury maddens Bacchus's tame tigers, who kill Argives; battle breaks out, and Capaneus kills Eunaeus.
scenes.stakes: Warriors on both sides die in an unplanned battle.

scenes.title: Amphiaraus Swallowed by Earth
scenes.summary: Amphiaraus, aided by Apollo, slaughters many foes until Apollo leaves him and the earth opens and takes him living to Tartarus.

alias_notes.explanation: Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene; also called Tegean and Maenalian for Arcadian places.
Roman name of Bacchus, also Lyaeus.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of how a great war grows from tiny bloodshed.
Concise insight into how fear makes anything believable.
Jupiter says fate, not Juno's will, ordains the war.

analysis.text: The book shows war set off by gods, fate and fury rather than by reason, even when mothers and sisters plead for peace.
Statius writes in the Flavian era, drawing on Roman epic traditions; the long catalogue of Boeotian towns imitates Homer's catalogue of ships.

legacy.text: The House of War, with Rage, Fear and Treachery as guards, influenced later allegorical halls, such as those in Spenser and Chaucer's Knight's Tale.

fun_facts.text: Statius's portrait of Mars's iron palace echoes Virgil and Valerius Flaccus, and was later admired by Dante, who placed Statius in Purgatory.

language_notes.text: Pelasgians: an old name for the Greeks, here the Argive army that has marched against Thebes (the Tyrian war).
The speedy Tegean is Mercury, called Tegean from Arcadia, where Mount Maenalus and the town of Tegea lie.
The Parrhasian is Callisto, turned into the Bear constellation, which never sets in the ocean; Parrhasia is in Arcadia.
Inachian means Argive, from Inachus, the river-god and first king of Argos.
The Argives are holding funeral games at the tomb of Opheltes, the child killed by a serpent, which the poem narrates earlier.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, probably 'the marching one'.
Tritonia is Minerva; Jupiter sarcastically says she alone would suffice for the Theban war.
Cyllenian: Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene. Aquilo is the north wind.
Mulciber (Vulcan) trapped his wife Venus and Mars in a net of chains when the Sun exposed their adultery.
Pelops' ivory shoulder, replaced after the gods mistakenly ate it, is the 'ivory arm'. Adrastus hopes the Nemean games will outshine Olympic ones at Elis and Arcadian rites.
The serpent that killed Archemorus and the Castalian shrine (Delphi) allude to Apollo's Pythian games; 'its own shade' and Lechaeum point to the Isthmian games near Corinth.
Avernus is the entrance to the underworld; 'refuse' means Adrastus will not consign the child wholly to death, but make him a star-like deity.
Inachian means Argive, from Inachus, the legendary first river-god and king of Argos.
Gradivus is a title of Mars; Ephyrean means Corinthian, from the old name Ephyre.
Ismenian means Theban, from the river Ismenus near Thebes.
Pisa, Pylos and Laconia are Greek regions; Panic imitates allied soldiers to make the report of a nearby enemy believable.
Inachian means Argive, from Inachus, the legendary first king and river-god of Argos; here it refers to the Argive army marching on Thebes.
Tyrian city means Thebes, which was founded by Cadmus, who came from Tyre in Phoenicia.
Refers to Semele, Bacchus's mother, destroyed by Jupiter's lightning when she asked to see him in his full glory. Juno tricked her into the request, and Jupiter had sworn by Styx to grant it.
Jupiter visited Danaë as golden rain, Callisto in the Parrhasian (Arcadian) grove, and Leda at Amyclae as a swan. Bacchus says he is gentler in love than in war.
Jupiter sewed the unborn Bacchus into his own thigh after Semele died, and so gave him a second birth.
Curetes were the armed attendants who guarded the infant Jupiter in Crete. Targes are light shields.
Lycurgus, king of Thrace, persecuted Bacchus. India was the scene of the god's legendary eastern triumph.
Bacchus lists gods whose homes Jupiter protected: Apollo's Delos, fixed in place for Latona; Minerva's Athens; Epaphus's Egypt; Mercury's Cyllene; and Jupiter's own Cretan Ida.
Hercules was begotten on Alcmena at Thebes, in a night Jupiter made longer. The bull is Jupiter, who carried off Europa, Agenor's daughter.
The Lapithae were destroyed by the Centaurs' war, and Calydon by Diana's boar. Jupiter says he allowed both punishments unwillingly.
Pentheus, king of Thebes, resisted Bacchus and was torn apart by the frenzied Bacchants, his own mother among them.
Aonian: poetic for Boeotian, the region around Thebes, named for Aon; Aonia is used throughout for Theban territory.
Pelasgians: an old name for the Greeks, here the Argive invaders; "tribes of Pelops" in the next sentence means the same.
Orion was a hunter killed after offending Diana (Artemis); the speaker hopes his son Dryas will not share that fate.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose."
Lapithaon and Alatreus are father and son, yet the son looks as old as the father, because the father was seduced young.
Asopos, a river god, was the father of Aegina, whom Jove carried off; he fought Jove in rage and was struck by lightning.
Glaucus was a fisherman who ate a magic herb, leapt into the sea and became a sea god with a fish's tail.
Narcissus, son of the river Cephisus, pined for his own reflection and was turned into the flower that bears his name.
Laius, Antigone's grandfather, was killed at a crossroads by his own son Oedipus, who did not know him; Phorbas was his charioteer.
"A common soldier" means Eteocles says he would gladly serve under another leader, so his speech is no mere command but courtesy toward allies.
Eteocles turns to address his absent brother Polynices, the "native enemy" who leads the Argive attack on Thebes.
"Danai" is another name for the Greeks, here the Argive army; "the Father" is Jove, who thunders against them.
Cirrha was the port serving Delphi, Apollo's oracle; its silence signals divine disfavour toward the Argive campaign.
Lycaon was a legendary Arcadian king turned into a wolf; Oenomaus was the king of Pisa killed in the chariot race with Pelops.
"Pelopean" means of Pelops, i.e. Greek, from the Peloponnese, which is named after him.
"Sidonian towers" means Theban towers, since Thebes' founder Cadmus came from Phoenicia, whose chief city was Sidon.
Amphion's fortress: Amphion, with his lyre, was said to have raised Thebes' walls, so the phrase means Thebes' defences.
Inachian means Argive, after Inachus, the river-god and legendary first king of Argos.
Phoebe is the Moon; Titan is the Sun, as a descendant of the Titans.
Olive branch entwined with dark wool is the mark of a suppliant seeking peace.
'Now the better sex' means the daughters, women, show more strength and courage than the men of the family.
Achaean is used here for Greek, here the Argive besiegers.
Cadmean means Theban, from Cadmus, the city's founder; the hero is Polynices.
Hyrcanians and Odrysians were distant, barbarian peoples, Jocasta's way of saying she could bear a stranger's savagery but not her son's.
Refers to Tydeus' earlier embassy to Thebes, where Eteocles' men ambushed him after a feigned welcome.
Achelous is the river of Tydeus' homeland, Aetolia; flowing backward is a proverbial impossibility.
Liber is Bacchus. His tigers once drew his chariot in his conquest of the East; Aonian means Boeotian, the region of Thebes.
Lyaeus, "the loosener", is a title of Bacchus; the citizens take the tigers' arrival as the god's own.
Amphiaraus is the Argive seer who foresaw his own doom; his charioteer's death is an ill omen for him.
Hercules, Semele and Harmonia are tied to Thebes: Hercules and Bacchus were born there, and Harmonia was Cadmus's wife. The Thebans would rather lose these places than suffer the tigers' deaths.
Pierian sisters are the Muses. Helicon is their mountain, and Aonia is Boeotia, so the war is "their own country's".
Bromian is from Bromius, "the roarer", a title of Bacchus.
Apollo's oracle guided Cadmus to found Thebes by following a heifer. Eunaeus claims the city is divinely sanctioned.
Legend says Amphion's lyre made stones move into place to build Thebes' walls.
Jove married Semele, daughter of Cadmus, and Gradivus (Mars) fathered Harmonia, hence the in-law claims. Alcides is Hercules.
Gradivus is Mars, god of war; his 'brother' is Apollo, both being gods fighting on the same side, here as fellow Olympians.
Tripod and bay (laurel) are the instruments of Apollo's oracle at Delphi; Phoebus is Apollo's title as god of light.
The fillet is a priestly headband; it reveals Lycoreus as a priest of Phoebus, whom Amphiaraus would not willingly have killed.
Asopus is a river god and Hypseus's father. The 'ashes of Giants' and his striving with Jove refer to myths of his riverbanks and his defiance of the king of gods.
Apollo disguises himself as the charioteer Haliacmon, a mortal from Lerna, to drive Amphiaraus's chariot.
Creon will rule Thebes after the war and forbid burial of the fallen enemy; Amphiaraus will escape this fate by being taken alive.
The 'triple baying' sentinel is Cerberus, the three-headed dog guarding the underworld.
The betrayed home refers to his wife Eriphyle, who betrayed him for a necklace; his son Alcmaeon will avenge him.
The brethren of Therapnae are Castor and Pollux; their fire is St Elmo's fire, a sailors' omen. Its flight from the sails was thought to foretell doom.

context_notes.text: Jupiter is angry because the Argive army is delaying the war against Thebes, which the gods have already destined.
Thrace, with Mount Haemus and the river Hebrus, was the traditional home of Mars and of warlike tribes.
Bellona is the Roman goddess of war, who often serves as the war-god's charioteer or companion.
Archemorus was the infant son of Lycurgus, killed by a serpent; the Nemean games were founded in his honour during the Argive march on Thebes.
Acrocorinthus is the high citadel hill of Corinth, which lies between two seas, the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf.
Panic is a personified attendant of Mars, the war god, who spreads groundless terror among armies.
Bacchus (the Greek Dionysus) was born at Thebes to Semele and Jupiter, so he feels a bond with the city.
Juno, Jupiter's wife, favoured Argos and Mycenae and hated Thebes, which was linked to Jupiter's lovers; Bacchus calls her his stepmother.
The Theban royal house of Labdacus, whose line includes Oedipus, was marked by crime, and Oedipus's sons Eteocles and Polynices are now at war.
Aonian is a poetic name for Theban, from Aonia, part of Boeotia. The darker age refers to later Theban disasters, which Jupiter postpones.
Eteocles holds the throne of Thebes and refuses to yield it to his brother Polynices, which is why the Argive army approaches.
Antigone is the daughter of Oedipus and sister of Eteocles and Polynices. Phorbas is her old guardian, formerly Laius' attendant.
Creon is Antigone's uncle and a Theban leader; his son Haemon bears a Sphinx on his crest, recalling Oedipus' defeat of the Sphinx.
Amphion was the legendary musician who built the walls of Thebes with his lyre; his is the Theban ancestral hero's emblem here.
Phocis was sacred to Phoebus Apollo, who slew the serpent Python near Delphi, hence the bay (laurel) and quiver emblems.
Eteocles is king of Thebes, holding the throne against his brother Polynices, who had agreed to alternate rule but was refused his turn.
The Asopus is the river of Boeotia, near Thebes, and is here also a river god who may oppose the invaders.
Hippomedon is one of the seven Argive champions against Thebes, known for his great size and strength.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, goddesses of vengeance. Oedipus, blind, had earlier cursed his sons.
Jocasta is mother of Polynices and Eteocles, and also wife of her son Oedipus, hence her guilt.
Tydeus is Polynices' Argive ally and father-in-law's champion; he opposes any peace that would waste the war.
Bacchus's followers wore vine and ivy and kept tame beasts in his honour.
Jocasta, mother of Polynices and Eteocles, had come to the Argive camp to seek peace.
Centaurs were half man, half horse, hence the "two lives" in the comparison.
Eunaeus is dressed as a delicate Bacchic priest, not a warrior.
Amphiaraus is the Argive seer and warrior, devoted to Apollo, who knows he is fated to die at Thebes.
Manto was a priestess and prophetess, daughter of the Theban seer Tiresias.
Tartarus and Avernus here name the underworld; Amphiaraus descends alive, as the earth closes above him.

literary_notes.text: Jupiter's nod shakes the stars and makes Atlas feel heavier, which shows his overwhelming power.
Jupiter sarcastically offers peace and kindness to a war-god, which is really a threat meant to shame Mars into action.
Light itself fears the dwelling, which shows how dark and menacing the house of Mars is.
Passion, Mischief, Fear, Treachery and Discord stand guard as sentinels, so the house of war is made of its own abstractions.
Even Jupiter would feel awe at Mars, so the war-god is shown as terrifying to Mercury.
Jupiter's fading anger is likened to a sea still swelling after the wind has dropped, showing that tension lingers.
Fear is made a skilled, shape-shifting agent of Mars, with countless voices and hands, turning an emotion into a character.
Absurd visions of two suns and marching forests show how panic distorts perception, and the narrator's 'alas' adds pity.
The terse statement sums up the scene: to frightened minds every rumour seems true.
The rush to arms is compared to a harbour in uproar at departure, with its sails and ropes, conveying hasty, emotional commitment to a journey of no return.
Bacchus's disordered garlands, fallen thyrsus and tears show him as an anxious suppliant, quite unlike his usual festive self.
Bacchus piles up questions about Jupiter's cruelty, and the brief clipped sentences convey his anguish and reproach.
Jupiter smiles at his son's jealousy, which lightens the tone, yet he claims to be ruled by fate, a limit even on his own power.
Bacchus's recovery is compared to drooping roses revived by gentler weather, which suits a god of nature and growth.
The plain is called "doomed to war" and "awaits the fury of the fray," signalling the coming slaughter.
Matrons showing children the glittering armour makes the coming war look like a spectacle, a poignant contrast to its later horror.
The cheering Thebans are compared to swans singing at the river Strymon as winter ends.
Antigone wishes her brothers had such concord, yet Eteocles and Polynices are fated to kill each other.
The river is given pride and joy, exhaling the ashes of his punishment, as a defeated god still proud.
Phorbas' wish to have died with Laius shows his loyalty and old grief, which colour his role as guide.
Eteocles arranging his troops is compared to a shepherd tenderly ordering his flock, suggesting careful, protective leadership.
The catalogue of ominous portents tells the reader that the Argive expedition is doomed.
Chance is called a "herald of doom" that scatters presages, as if it were a messenger of the gods.
The cattle hesitating at the stream until the lead bull crosses mirrors the soldiers following Hippomedon's example.
Natural rocks, slopes and mounds serve as walls and trenches, as if nature itself helped the Argives and so ending the scene with a quiet, ironic calm before war.
The narrator opens by confessing the difficulty of describing the panic, heightening it.
Comparing Jocasta to the oldest Fury casts her grief as terrifying and hints at her family's curse.
Lions sated after slaughter mirror the soldiers' wrath softening, suggesting their fierceness is appetite, not principle.
Winds contending for the sea picture the crowd's mood being seized back by Tydeus's speech.
Erinys seizes the moment and sows strife like a farmer, showing the Fury's hand behind the turn.
The gentle, wine-sipping tigers are described at length, which sharpens the shock of their return to savagery.
The tigers' rush is likened to twin lightning-bolts trailing through the clouds like long hair.
The wounded tigers' human-like wails and leaning on beloved walls make them pitiable.
The growing wind shows how a little bloodshed swells into a vast battle.
The narrator addresses Eunaeus directly, expressing pity and reproach.
Capaneus is a lion eagerly spying prey and heedless of wounds, conveying his reckless confidence.
Places across the world mourn Eunaeus, making his death a grand lament.
His knowledge of death gives him strength, yet he would read the heavens better if he had leisure; the seer becomes a slaughterer.
The narrator breaks in, lamenting how the healer and prophet has become a killer.
Comparing his sword to plague or a baleful star presents his killing as a deadly, almost cosmic force.
A landslide sweeping away fields and oaks conveys the chariot's destructive, unstoppable weight.
Apollo's hidden tears and the groaning chariot show grief at losing his servant.
Warring ships united by a storm parallel the soldiers' enmity vanishing in shared terror at the earthquake.
